'''Aurelia Skipwith Giacometto''' is an American [[lawyer|attorney]], businesswoman, and [[biologist]] who served as the 17th director of the [[United States Fish and Wildlife Service]] from 2019 to 2021. She was confirmed by the [[United States Senate|Senate]] as director on December 12, 2019, by a 52–39 vote, and is the first black director of the [[Fish and Wildlife Service]].<ref name="Bloomberg">{{cite news |last1=Scott |first1=Dean |title=Aurelia Skipwith Confirmed to Run U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (1) |url=https://news.bloombergenvironment.com/environment-and-energy/aurelia-skipwith-confirmed-to-run-u-s-fish-and-wildlife-service |accessdate=8 January 2020 |work=news.bloombergenvironment.com |date=December 12, 2019 |language=en}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Skipwith was born and raised in [[Indianapolis]], [[Indiana]], the oldest of nine children. Skipwith's family eventually relocated to [[Columbus, Mississippi]]. Skipwith's father served in the [[United States Navy]] and [[United States Army Reserve]]. Her grandfather was a farmer in [[Mississippi]].<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-04-21|title=An Interview with Aurelia Skipwith Director–U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service|url=https://www.boone-crockett.org/interview-aurelia-skipwith-director-us-fish-and-wildlife-service|access-date=2020-07-23|website=Boone and Crockett Club|language=en}}</ref>

Skipwith received a Bachelor of Science degree in biology from [[Howard University]] in 2003, a Master of Science in [[molecular genetics]] from [[Purdue University]], and a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of Kentucky Rosenberg College of Law]].<ref>{{cite web|last1=Doyle|first1=Michael|date=December 12, 2019|title=INTERIOR: Skipwith confirmed as Fish and Wildlife Service director|url=https://www.eenews.net/stories/1061793089|accessdate=8 January 2020|website=www.eenews.net|language=en}}</ref>

== Early career ==
Skipwith began her career at [[Monsanto]] in 2006 as a lab technician, and worked her way to a sustainable agriculture partnership manager.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Aurelia Skipwith|url=https://departmentofinfluence.org/person/aurelia-skipwith/|access-date=2020-07-12|website=Department of Influence}}</ref> Following her work at Monsanto, Skipwith completed law school and had a brief career as a research and legal intern at the [[United States Department of Agriculture (USDA), USA|United States Department of Agriculture]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Aurelia Skipwith is Confirmed as Next Director of U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service|url=https://protecttheharvest.com/news/aurelia-skipwith-is-confirmed-as-next-director-of-u.s-fish-and-wildlife-service/|access-date=2020-07-12|website=Protect The Harvest|date=12 December 2019 |language=en}}</ref> She also served as an [[intellectual property]] consultant for the [[United States Agency for International Development]].<ref name=":1" />

For a period of time, Skipwith worked at [[Alltech]], an organization based in [[Nicholasville, Kentucky]] which specializes in animal nutrition and algae production. She later co-founded AVC Global, an agricultural supply [[blockchain company]] in early-2016.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Nsehe|first=Mfonobong|title=Riyada Group Partners AVC Global To Create An African Agricultural Supply Blockchain Company|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/mfonobongnsehe/2018/12/01/riyada-group-partners-avc-global-to-create-an-african-agricultural-supply-blockchain-company/|access-date=2020-07-23|website=Forbes|language=en}}</ref>

== Trump administration ==

From April 2017 to January 2020, Skipwith served as deputy assistant secretary fish, wildlife and parks of the Department of the Interior.

[[File:Aurelia Skipwith.jpg|120px|thumb|right|Aurelia Skipwith as Deputy Assistant Secretary for Fish and Wildlife and Parks]]

Skipwith served as the director of the [[United States Fish and Wildlife Service]] starting in January 2020. Her appointment was widely supported by conservatives and opposed by environmentalists due to her ties to the pesticide industry and her support of the Trump administration's efforts to roll back environmental protections.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2019-09-11|title=Trump's Fish and Wildlife pick under scrutiny for previous work for Monsanto|url=http://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2019/sep/11/auriela-skipwith-fish-and-wildlife-monsanto|access-date=2021-01-16|website=the Guardian|language=en}}</ref> The [[Center for Biological Diversity]] stated "Aurelia Skipwith has been working in the Trump administration all along to end protections for billions of migratory birds, gut endangered species safeguards and eviscerate national monuments. Skipwith will always put the interests of her old boss Monsanto and other polluters ahead of America's wildlife and help the most anti-environmental administration in history do even more damage."<ref>{{Cite web|title=Trump Nominates Pesticide Industry Insider to Run U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service|url=https://www.biologicaldiversity.org/news/press_releases/2018/aurelia-skipwith-10-23-2018.php|access-date=2021-01-15|website=www.biologicaldiversity.org}}</ref>

[[File:Vice President Mike Pence Participates in a Ceremonial Swearing-in (49347561466).jpg|thumb|Vice President [[Mike Pence]] swears Aurelia Skipwith Giacometto as the Director of the [[U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service]] Monday, Jan. 6, 2020]]

Under Skipwith's direction, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service generated controversy by not granting Monarch butterflies protection,<ref>{{Cite news|last=Einhorn|first=Catrin|date=2020-12-15|title=Monarch Butterflies Qualify for Endangered List. They Still Won't Be Protected.|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/12/15/climate/monarch-butterflies-endangered-species-list.html|access-date=2021-01-15|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> requiring entries in the Federal Duck Stamp Contest to include a hunting theme,<ref>{{Cite news|last=Hauser|first=Christine|date=2020-10-13|title=What Makes a Good Duck Painting? The Government Suggests Some Hunting|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/10/13/us/duck-stamp-contest-hunting.html|access-date=2021-01-15|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> weakening rules against the killing of birds by oil and gas companies and others,<ref>{{Cite news|last=Friedman|first=Lisa|date=2020-01-30|title=Trump Administration Moves to Relax Rules Against Killing Birds|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/01/30/climate/trump-bird-deaths.html|access-date=2021-01-15|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> and massively reducing the protected habitat of threatened owls.<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Friedman|first1=Lisa|last2=Einhorn|first2=Catrin|date=2021-01-13|title=Trump Opens Habitat of a Threatened Owl to Timber Harvesting|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/01/13/climate/trump-spotted-owl.html|access-date=2021-01-15|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

She left office on January 19, 2021.<ref>{{cite tweet |user=USFWSDirector |number=1351695366027173897
|first=Aurelia |last=Skipwith |date=January 19, 2021 |title=Our history does not define who we are today, it is the inspiration for what we can achieve.  |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210120005809/https://twitter.com/USFWSDirector/status/1351695366027173897 |archive-date=January 20, 2021}}</ref>

== Post-Trump administration ==
[[File:CPAC Hungary 2025 (112).jpg|120px|thumb|right|Skipwith at [[Conservative Political Action Conference|CPAC]] in Hungary of 2025]]

She became the Secretary of the [[Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality]] (LDEQ) in January 2024. <ref>{{cite web|title=Office of the Secretary Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality|url=https://deq.louisiana.gov/directory/office/office-of-the-secretary|access-date=4 September 2024}} </ref> She left office on May 2, 2025, after accepting a position with Earth and Water Law in Washington, DC.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Governor Jeff Landry Addresses the Future Leadership of the Department of Environmental Quality {{!}} Office of Governor Jeff Landry |url=https://gov.louisiana.gov/news/4845 |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=gov.louisiana.gov |language=en}}</ref>

She spoke at [[Conservative Political Action Conference|CPAC]] in Hungary of 2025.

== Personal life ==
Skipwith Giacometto married [[Leo Giacometto]], a former member of the [[Montana Legislature]] and chief of staff to former Senator [[Conrad Burns]]. Giacometto was a co-founder of AVC Global and who worked as a lobbyist in the agriculture sector.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Okeson|first=Sarah|date=2019-01-09|title=Polluters' Friend to Take Reins of Fish and Wildlife Service|url=https://www.dcreport.org/2019/01/09/polluters-friend-poised-to-take-the-reins-of-fish-and-wildlife-service/|access-date=2020-07-23|website=[[DCReport]]|language=en-US}}</ref> He was previously married to Mildred Echeverria for twenty-six years, with whom he shared two children and two grandchildren.<ref>{{Citation |title=Leo Giacometto |date=2026-06-06 |work=Wikipedia |url=https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Leo_Giacometto&oldid=1358097295 |access-date=2026-06-06 |language=en}}</ref>
